newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower, take profits after data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower, take profits after data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower on Wednesday after fresh, stronger-than-expected data poured cold water on the market's bullishness and prompted some profit-taking, analysts said.

The 6-3/4-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 9/32 at 100-18/32. Its yield, which touched a fresh seven-month low of 6.64 percent early in the session, rebounded somewhat to close at 6.70 percent.

The selling bout was broad-based, ranging from hedge funds to portfolio managers to retailers. But analysts said foreign players, mainly from the Middle East, were said to be the most active sellers during the day.
"We saw some foreigners selling here after the mid-morning data," said an analyst at a U.S. investment bank who asked not to be named.
"There was talk of some heavy selling orders, ranging from $500 miliion to $1.0 billion, in the middle of the yield curve, mainly 10-year (notes)," the analyst added.

The market started the day on a bullish note after the government announced in its first estimate of third quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) that the economy grew at a 2.2-percent pace against a 4.7-percent rate in the final second-quarter figure.
The 30-year T-bond rallied about half a point shortly after the number was released.

"The GDP was a nice number, particularly the mix of very weak final sales, which was quite constructive for the market," said Cary Leahey, senior financial market economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
But the market's optimism did not hold for too long.
Prices trimmed gains and marched toward negative territory after the Commerce Department reported sales of new single-family homes fell 0.5 percent in September to an annual rate of 816,000 units.
Although homes sales dropped, analysts said the overall number remained at a lofty level. The 816,000 figure is the second highest since 857,000 in April of 1986.
The market's flirting with negative territory was complete when the Federal Reserve announced its Beige Book at noon.

Analysts said some aspects of the report were seen as bearish for bonds. In a nutshell, the Beige Book said the economy is growing at a moderate pace, labor markets remain tight, but no inflation threat is looming.

"People used small bits of information as an excuse to take profits," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at C.S. First Boston Corp. "This is a classic case of profit-taking after a huge move," he added.
On Tuesday, bonds rallied two full points after the third quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI) rose a lower-than-expected 0.6 percent.

Analysts said the announcement of the Treasury's quarterly refunding auctions on Wednesday also weighed on prices. The government will sell $38.5 billion in securities divided in three-, 10- and 30-year maturities.
The auctions will take place next week. The Treasury will also offer $13.0 billion in 34-day cash management bills on November 13.
"We'll be able to go through the auctions, but it might be more difficult than we once thought," said a trader at a U.S. commercial bank.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.01 percent. The six-month bill rate was unchanged at 5.08 percent. The year bill rate was up one basis point at 5.17 percent.

The two-year note closed down 3/32 at 100-4/32, yielding 5.81 percent. The five-year note traded off 4/32 at 100-15/32 to yield 6.14 percent. The ten-year note closed down 5/32 at 100-21/32, yielding 6.41 percent.
